name: Kris Sidial🇺🇸
zh_summary: 大型市場波動往往需要雙向行動，因為另一方參與者最終會平倉，儲存能量加速波動。含義不明確的灰色催化劑通過吸引對立觀點來維持這種動態，直到資本約束迫使交易。例子包括2020年3月COVID期間抄底者和波動率賣方助長進一步下跌，以及2021年1月迷因狂熱中GameStop和AMC的空頭為上漲增添燃料。
en_summary: Large market moves often need two-way action because participants on the other side eventually unwind, storing energy that accelerates the move. Gray catalysts with unclear implications sustain this by attracting opposing views until capital constraints force transactions. Examples include COVID in March 2020 where dip buyers and vol sellers fueled further declines, and meme mania in January 2021 with GameStop and AMC where shorts added fuel to the surge.
ko_summary: 대형 시장 움직임은 종종 양방향 행동이 필요하다. 반대편 참가자들이 결국 포지션을 청산하면서 에너지를 저장해 움직임을 가속화하기 때문이다. 함의가 불명확한 회색 촉매는 자본 제약으로 거래가 강제될 때까지 반대 견해를 끌어들여 이를 지속시킨다. 예로는 2020년 3월 COVID 때 하락 매수자와 변동성 매도자가 추가 하락을 부추긴 경우와 2021년 1월 밈 열풍에서 GameStop과 AMC의 공매도가 급등에 연료를 더한 경우가 있다.
text:
By nature of being a vol trader, I’ve studied many different market crashes. Not just the common ones in the U.S., but episodes like Britain in 1720, Vienna in 1873, and the Dutch tulip mania of 1637.

There are some interesting behavioral takeaways that aren’t entirely intuitive unless you participate in markets every single day.

One of the biggest for me is that large market moves often need two-way action to develop. Behaviorally, you need participants willing to take the other side, because their eventual need to unwind can help accelerate the move. It’s almost like storing energy that gets released later. To create that dynamic, a “gray catalyst” can be particularly powerful one whose implications aren’t immediately black and white. 

Here are two examples that helped produce massive moves in opposite directions that had gray area headlines that led to that two way flow. 

COVID (March 2020): What often gets lost in the sauce is that many participants were aggressively betting against the idea that COVID would be severely disruptive. As stocks fell, they bought the dip and sold vol. When stocks kept falling and vol kept rising, some of those positions became fuel for the next leg of the move as participants were forced to unwind.

Looking back, the outcome seems obvious. In real time, the eventual scale of the disruption was far from clear. There was HOPE that it would pass quickly. Headlines about potential treatments, policy support, or a less severe impact repeatedly

BREAKING: The S&P Global US Manufacturing PMI index rose +0.1 point in October, to 56.0, its highest level since May 2022.

This exceeded expectations of a -0.4 point decline.

The improvement was particularly driven by job growth, which rose to its strongest level since March 2012.

Meanwhile, the Services PMI index fell -0.9 points, to 57.9, its 2nd-highest level in 4 years.

This brought the Composite PMI index down -0.8 points, to 57.6, also its 2nd-highest in 4 years.

Despite the slight decline, these readings point to GDP growth of +5.0% at an annualized rate in Q4 2026, following projected growth of +4.0% in Q3 2026.

text:
Last week started with Trump desperately attempting to talk down the markets for oil and refined products, such as diesel fuel. Among other things, Trump’s spin was that more oil is coming out of the Strait of Hormuz than before the war. This spin even made the lead story on the front page of The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday: “More Oil Is Now Coming Out of the Persian Gulf Than Before the Iran War.”

But there were many problems with that spin, including the fact that the price of Brent crude shot up by 7% after the Wall Street Journal’s lead story appeared. The narrative just didn’t make any sense. If there is so much oil coming out of the Strait, why does the price of Brent keep hitting new highs with each passing day? Two plus two does not equal five.

After the most recent price surge, Trump was forced to switch stories. On his social media platform, Truth Social, he threw in the towel on high prices and is now blaming them on Iran. But this narrative makes absolutely no sense either, since it was Trump’s war of choice against Iran that made the Strait functionally inoperative and caused the price of Brent to soar by 60% since the start of the war.

zh_summary: @Ksidiii：分享沽空數據圖的人忽略背後資金流：多數機構並非直接看淡押注，而是提供資產負債表的銀行要求客戶增加空頭部位以放寬保證金要求。
en_summary: @Ksidiii: short interest charts miss the flows: most shops are not making outright short bets; banks providing balance sheet for speculative bets are asking clients to post more short exposure to ease margin requirements.
ko_summary: @Ksidiii: 공매도 잔고 차트를 공유하는 이들은 자금 흐름을 놓친다. 대부분은 순수 숏 베팅이 아니라, 투기적 베팅에 대차대조표를 제공하는 은행이 증거금 완화를 위해 고객에게 더 많은 숏 노출을 요구하는 것.
text:
Everyone who keeps sharing these short interest charts is missing the flows behind them. Most shops are not taking outright short bets. This is another effort to ease margin requirements across the street: banks providing balance sheet for more speculative bets are asking clients to post more short exposure.

The sequence on the street looks like this:

HF manager: “I want more margin.”

Bank: “Things look risky in public AI bets, and we’re already lending a lot against private AI bets. For some clients, we’ll extend more financing, but only if they add more short exposure to improve their collateral scores.”

HF manager: “Okay, I’ll short more stock against my main bet.”

That is how you end up with short exposures that look astronomically high while many end users remain heavily long tech. The additional shorts are supporting the financing of their main bets.

Which also tells the bigger story on why raw equity financing rates haven’t blown out the way they did ahead of the big SpaceX IPO in June, despite the fact that lending is slowing.

zh_summary: （由@elonmusk轉發）@EvaFox講述2002年初Elon準備創立SpaceX時發現Tom Mueller扛著80磅火箭引擎，這是業餘愛好者建造的最大液體燃料引擎，推力達13,000磅。Elon問他能否建造更大的，他們繪製了第一枚SpaceX火箭，Tom成為第1號員工並建造了Merlin、Kestrel和Draco引擎。
en_summary: (Reposted by @elonmusk) @EvaFox recounts in early 2002 Elon preparing to launch SpaceX found Tom Mueller with an 80-pound rocket engine, the largest amateur liquid-fuel engine with 13,000 pounds thrust. Elon asked if he could build something bigger, they sketched the first SpaceX rocket, Tom became employee #1 and built Merlin, Kestrel and Draco engines.
ko_summary: (@elonmusk에 의해 리포스트됨) @EvaFox는 2002년 초 Elon이 SpaceX를 출범시키려던 중 80파운드 로켓 엔진을 들고 있는 Tom Mueller를 발견했다고 말합니다. 이는 아마추어가 만든 최대 액체 연료 엔진으로 13,000파운드 추력을 가졌습니다. Elon은 더 큰 것을 만들 수 있는지 물었고, 그들은 첫 SpaceX 로켓을 스케치했으며, Tom은 1호 직원이 되어 Merlin, Kestrel, Draco 엔진을 만들었습니다.
text:
In early 2002, Elon was preparing to launch SpaceX and searching for the people who could help him build a rocket from scratch. One Sunday in January 2002, he walked into a friend's rented warehouse in Huntington Beach and found Tom Mueller holding an 80-pound rocket engine on his shoulder, trying to bolt it to a frame. It was the largest liquid-fuel engine any amateur had ever built, with 13,000 pounds of thrust, made in Tom's spare time. 

Elon asked the main question  “Could you build something bigger?”

The next Sunday Elon came to his house. It was Super Bowl Sunday; they watched maybe one play, because they were too busy sketching the first SpaceX rocket.

Tom became SpaceX employee #1, and the man who built engines on weekends went on to build Merlin, Kestrel and Draco. 

Elon saw a person, not a résumé, someone who built rockets with his own hands simply because he loved them.

en_summary: Puru Saxena notes that drawdowns are normal for the S&P 500, with ~80-95% of time below prior peaks historically, and advises staying the course for long-term equity returns as volatility is the price of admission.
ko_summary: Puru Saxena가 S&P 500 드로다운이 정상적이며 역사적으로 이전 고점 아래 시간의 약 80-95%를 보낸다고 지적하고, 변동성이 입장료이므로 장기 주식 수익을 위해 코스를 유지하라고 조언함.
text:
Drawdowns are the norm. New highs are the exception.

Historically the S&P 500 has spent ~80–95% of its time below a prior peak. Since 1871, 82% of months were underwater (price basis). Since 1950, only about 7% of trading days were at record highs.

Volatility is the price of admission. You cannot earn equity-like long-term returns with bond-like volatility; there is no free lunch. The temporary discomfort of being below your high-water mark is the cost of capturing the upside over decades.

That’s why staying the course matters for investors:

• Markets trend higher over time, but the path is jagged. Recoveries eventually erase most drawdowns. 
• Selling during declines locks in losses and risks missing the rebound. 
• The bigger risk is interrupting compounding by trying to avoid normal volatility.

Being underwater is uncomfortable but expected. The investors who do best treat drawdowns as the entry fee, not a reason to exit. Stay invested and let the long-term maths work.

ko_summary: (@Jason이 리포스트) @theallinpod는 Palo Alto Networks CEO @nikesharora가 사이버 공황이 막 시작됐으며 미지급 기술 부채로 인해 문제가 10일마다보다 훨씬 빠르게 발생하고 있다고 말하며 가상 패치와 경계 방어를 논의한다.
text:
Palo Alto Networks CEO: The Cyber Panic Is Just Getting Started

@Jason:

“There's a cyber panic. What's going on? Is this an acute issue or is this a harbinger of things to come? And is this going to happen every 10 days?”

@nikesharora:

“Jason, I think 10 days is too long. I think these things are going to happen much faster than every 10 days.

I think part of the challenge we're seeing is we've been talking about technology debt that we all have to pay sooner than later.

And what's happened is people have not paid attention to the idea that they have to go fix their stuff.

We found out about this a few days ago. We've scanned everything in our infrastructure to make sure that there were no issues. We made sure that our products had patches available for our customers who deploy them.

So there's two ways to solve this problem, right?

One, you can go in and patch the vulnerability. You can go in, find the code, patch what has been given to you by PHP, and make it work.

The other is you can actually put it in a perimeter defense product like ours, or Cloudflare has one, or other firewalls have one.

If you put the patch there, it's a virtual patch, so any attacker trying to access that vulnerability gets stopped at the perimeter because we know what they're looking for.

Guess what? The phones keep ringing every day, and the conversation always is, ‘Now how do I get out of this? Because I'm tired of getting punched in the face every morning when I wake up.’”

Grant Cardone says Wall Street's real estate giants are trapped by redemptions, turning his retail money into an advantage

"I bought through all the cycles, and I have great relationships with the sellers, and they know I'm a closer. They know that my money is different than their money."

"It is basically a dozen to 15, maybe 25 different guys. Big, giant, enormous investment companies. They just trade. Starwood goes to Blackstone, Blackstone goes to Goldman. They're just flipping it to one another."

"All those guys are sidelined. They have redemption issues. They have pension funds saying, I want my money back. It's been 5 years, dude. I'm done."

"The institutions are all kind of trapped right now. And then there's this guy Grant Cardone that was going to retail investors and never went to their well."

"I have this money that was frowned upon that is now like, oh, your money's perfect. It's discretionary. It's really cheap money. I probably have access to the cheapest money in the world."

text:
Grant Cardone on why his Bitcoin deal beats Saylor's 12%: 8% plus half the upside, instead of 12% and none

"When we add the Bitcoin, we actually added our pref back. We paid cash for the Bitcoin and put $100 million down on the real estate."

"We offered an 8% pref on that deal and went 50-50 on the Bitcoin. I promised eight to the investors. Over ten years, I owe them their money back plus 80%, and then we split everything above that."

"He said I'm greedy. He says, you're greedy, you want a 50-50. I'm like, I thought you said Bitcoin was going to zero, Peter."

"I'm basically using Saylor's 12, because his 12 is basically a 12 and a zero. It's 12% and no upside. Mine is 8% with a 50% upside on Bitcoin."

"We raised more money on the 8% pref and the 50-50 than we've raised on any deal I've ever done."

text:
Great thoughts here from @TheStalwart — I agree it’s not at all obvious whether the AI era will create a more or less centrist information environment. It’s going to depend crucially on what new economic model for producing news emerges, how much AI models end up personalizing to users’ views, and more.

We need way more people working on this! Some questions:

—what can we learn from the evolution of SEO and google to reason about how AI systems should take on news

—what does the news ecosystem look like in a world where people consume news via AI?

—what would an “optimal” ai system for political news look like. When would it tailor to a users’ preferences and when would it not?

A great area for political economy to start studying in much more detail.

“Two years ago we had about 200 interns, and what we saw was those interns were really the first fully AI native. If you took AI away from them, I don't think they would be able to work.

I think they know how to use the tools better than us. It's just like if you took Google away from me over the last 10 years, how would I learn anything? That's where they reach first. And we actually saw the managers that had interns that summer adopt AI faster.

So this past year, we decided we're going to hire a thousand interns. For a 5,000 person company. Over the course of the year.

It's just been amazing, because of the number of ideas that come from the interns. With AI, fewer people experiment faster, so having more ideas is great. And just seeing the way they use AI: they need to fill out a form, they reach for AI. And I still find myself, there are so many things where I'm like, 'Oh wait, I've just been doing this manually still.'”
